title: A well-made head
hookLine: better a well-made head than a well-filled one (Essays 1.26)
last: WHAT FEELS LIKE NATURE IS OFTEN CUSTOM.

lines: NO HELP WITH A REAL CHOICE.
cards: A trivia night at a bar. One team has a member who knows every capital, every element, every year a war ended. They win.
Later that week, the same person is asked to help a friend decide whether to take a job in another city, and has nothing to offer but more facts. A head can be very full and still not very useful.
In a long essay on how to raise a child, Montaigne draws exactly this line, in one plain phrase.

teach.b: First, the line. When choosing a tutor for a child, Montaigne says, look for one with a well-made head rather than a well-filled one.
Both would be good, he allows, but character and understanding matter more than learning.
Second, the funnel. Teachers, he complains, keep shouting into children's ears as if pouring into a funnel, and the child's only job is to repeat what was said.
He wants the opposite: let the student taste things, choose, and tell them apart. Sometimes the tutor opens the way; sometimes he lets the student open it.
And he puts it bluntly: knowing something by heart is not knowing it. Third, the bees.
Bees go from flower to flower taking what they like, but the honey they make is all their own; it's no longer thyme or marjoram.
A student should do the same with what they borrow from books: turn it into their own judgment. Fourth, the test. How do you know someone has learned?
Not by what they can recite.

teach.h: PROOF IS IN HOW YOU LIVE.
teach.b: By how they live. Montaigne has a homely picture for it: if food comes back up just as it went down, it was never digested. Learning that comes out word for word hasn't been taken in.
Away from the classroom, a well-made head can belong to the friend who knows few capitals but asks the one question that helps you decide.

how: Readers of Montaigne's essay on the education of children take its line about a well-made head as a case for teaching judgment over memorization.

o: a mind that can judge well, not one stuffed with facts
a sharp memory that can repeat any lesson word for word
a strong, healthy body, trained before the mind is

games.q: Montaigne on learning: tap the pairs.
p: a well-made head, not a well-filled one
make honey that's all their own
food that comes back the same

s: Montaigne says knowing by heart is knowing
he says the opposite: knowing something by heart is not knowing it.
Montaigne says the bees' honey is no longer thyme or marjoram
they take from many flowers, but the honey is all theirs. so with what a student borrows.
Montaigne wants the tutor to fill the child with as many facts as possible
he wants a tutor with a well-made head, who lets the child taste, choose and judge.

games.q: you're choosing a tutor for a child. one has read everything. the other has fewer books but sound judgment. what does Montaigne advise?
o: the one with sound judgment, a well-made head.
no tutor; let the child teach himself.
games.why: both would be good, he allows, but he'd rather a well-made head than a well-filled one: understanding and character before learning.

practice: Pick one idea from these days on the path that you could recite but maybe couldn't explain: water, the runaway horse, custom, different roads.
Put it in your own words, in your head, as if telling a twelve-year-old at the kitchen table, with no quoting. If it falls apart, that's useful too; try again, plainer.

wordCard.voice: A well-made head. Montaigne's picture of a good mind: not stuffed with facts, but able to judge, like bees turning flowers into honey of their own. Today's word.

orig.note: French: a well-made head, from Montaigne's line on choosing a tutor.

carryVoice: Your line: well made, not full. The honey belongs to the bees, whatever flowers it came from. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Essays 1.26, Of the education of children (a tutor with a well-made rather than well-filled head; teachers pouring as into a funnel; let the student taste, choose and discern; to know by heart is not to know; the bees and their honey; undigested food as a sign of learning not taken in)
